evidence.title: High-power radiatively cooled thermoelectric generator for diurnal waste heat harvesting
evidence.abstract: Governed by the second law of thermodynamics, waste heat generation is inevitable and has been a major source of energy loss and environmental concern in human society. Harvesting waste heat into useful energy has thus become a paramount priority, but has remained challenging with efficiency and cost constraints. Thermoelectric generators (TEGs), which convert heat into electricity whenever there is a temperature difference, play a crucial role in waste heat harvesting. However, sustaining the temperature difference for uninterrupted and high-power density electricity generation is a major challenge in TEGs to achieve practical applications due to the thermal equilibrium. Here, we demonstrate a diurnal waste heat harvester by integrating a high-power radiative cooling film as the cool end of TEGs to enable a large and continuous temperature difference. Significant voltage increase from 30.0 mV to 65.7 mV was achieved, leading to a dramatic power density enhancement of 4.8 times from 35.2 mW m−2 to 168.6 mW m−2. In an open zone, an ultra-high power density of 2.76 W m−2 was achieved at a heat source temperature of 80 °C, exceeding the performance of state-of-the-art radiatively cooled TEGs. More importantly, a portable and foldable thermal energy harvesting prototype composed of 24 TEGs arranged in an array has been constructed. When attached to a hot object (e.g. a car engine hood), it can output 5 V to charge personal electronics (e.g. a cellphone), making it a promising practical device for harvesting waste heat in a wide range of outdoor applications.

evidence.title: Impacts of De‐NOx system layouts of a diesel passenger car on exhaust emission factors and monetary penalty
evidence.abstract: Abstract Automobile emissions are significantly dependent on the after‐treatment system performance, which is partly determined by exhaust temperature. Regarding diesel passenger cars, after‐treatment systems generally include diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC), diesel particulate filter (DPF), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR). The layouts affect their temperature variations because of the heat loss and thermal capacity of tailpipes and after‐treatment systems. As for the original layout of DOC+DPF+SCR, nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions are the main concerns of diesel vehicle emissions, especially under cold‐start conditions. Ammonia Creation and Conversion Technology (ACCT) system shows excellent performance of reducing cold‐start NOx emissions; additionally, the damage costs of individual exhaust emissions are different greatly, which may change the priority of emission reductions when considering monetary penalty. In this article, the impacts of the after‐treatment system layouts on the exhaust emission reductions were investigated based on a diesel passenger car; additionally, SCR and ACCT systems as the De‐NOx devices were adopted individually in corresponding scenarios; the after‐treatment system layouts were assessed from the viewpoints of both emission factors and monetary penalty. The results indicated that the ACCT system presented much better NOx reduction effectiveness than SCR system over different layouts. NOx reduction efficiency was very sensitive to vehicle operation conditions over the upstream layouts of NOx reduction devices. The layout‐1 of DOC+ACCT+DPF showed the lowest global emission factors from the diesel passenger car. DPF was much easier to achieve regeneration under the original layout conditions due to its shortest distance to the engine. The layout‐2 of ACCT+DOC+DPF had the minimum monetary penalty factor of exhaust emissions from this diesel passenger car.

evidence.title: Optimized nanofluid coolants enhance thermal performance in ruffled fin automotive radiators.
evidence.abstract: Nanofluids offer superior heat transfer compared to conventional automotive coolants, with further improvements achievable through particle hybridization and particle shape effects. This study numerically investigates the thermal performance of a ruffled-fin radiator using ternary hybrid nanofluids composed of ZnO, Al 2 O 3 , TiO 2 , MWCNTs, graphene, Fe, Cu, and Ag nanoparticles at varying volume fractions. Combinations such as Fe/Cu/Ag, Fe/Cu/ZnO, and Ag/Al 2 O 3 /TiO 2 enhanced convective heat transfer, as reflected in increased Nusselt numbers and overall heat transfer coefficients. Increasing the volume fraction reduced outlet coolant temperature, with an optimal nanofluid achieving a 44.6% temperature drop at the engine outlet. The performance index, defined as a composite measure of heat transfer and cooling efficiency, decreased by 5.8-11.7% across the eight ternary nanofluids, with non-metallic oxides exhibiting the smallest reduction. These results demonstrate the role of ternary hybrid nanofluids in improving radiator cooling while indicating efficiency trade-offs at higher volume fractions.

evidence.title: Directional thermal emission enables efficient energy savings.
evidence.abstract: Thermal radiation, a fundamental heat transfer mechanism, is crucial for energy exchange across various applications. However, conventional radiative heat transfer systems rely on omnidirectional thermal radiation, causing energy dissipation in undesired directions and limiting radiative heat transfer efficiency. Here, we show that perfectly matched directional thermal emission between an emitter and absorber can reach a theoretical efficiency up to 100%. In a parallel-plate configuration, replacing a conventional system with a customized directional system raises efficiency from 29% to 100%. We further experimentally demonstrate directional radiative heat transfer realizes substantial energy savings of 67.8% in vacuum and 28.7% in non-vacuum conditions. Moreover, directional radiative heat transfer enables efficient heating in diverse scenarios, including vehicle heating, car paint drying, human body heating, and rail car thawing, achieving 17-46% energy savings. Our work highlights the broad applicability and energy-saving potential of directional radiative heat transfer, opening new avenues for efficient energy utilization.

evidence.title: Optimization of automotive HVAC performance and passenger comfort through intelligent algorithms.
evidence.abstract: Optimizing passenger thermal comfort while maintaining energy efficiency remains a critical challenge in automotive climate control. This study investigates the complex thermal interaction between a passenger and a car seat, introducing a novel technique for direct thermal management through the vehicle's heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system. An experimental setup was developed using evaporator coils integrated beneath seat surfaces, addressing a significant gap in the literature regarding two-way (heating and cooling) seat thermal management. Artificial Neural Networks were employed to model the ambiguous system parameters and to predict thermal performance. The results show an excellent predictive accuracy with Mean Squared Error of 1.29E-02 and correlation coefficient of 0.99659. The average deviations were under -0.21% for cooling capacity, -0.02% for heating capacity and 0.38% for coefficient of performance. These results show that the integration of intelligent algorithms into modified heating, ventilation, and air conditioning architectures significantly improves occupant comfort and system efficiency, thereby providing a powerful data-driven framework for next-generation automotive climate control solutions.

1.1 The Crisis of the Von Neumann Bottleneck

The history of computing has been defined by a singular, persistent constraint: the physical limitation of information storage. From the earliest magnetic core memories to modern solid-state arrays, the fundamental paradigm has remained unchanged. Data is treated as a physical object—a sequence of magnetized grains or trapped electrons—that must be generated, moved, written, and maintained. This "containment model" of information has led to the Von Neumann bottleneck, where the speed of processing vastly outstrips the speed of retrieval, and the energy cost of maintaining data entropy threatens the scalability of planetary computation.

As we transition into an era of exascale computing and the burgeoning Internet of Things (IoT), the volume of data is expanding at a rate that physical storage media cannot sustain. The "Crisis of Storage" is not merely a question of capacity; it is a question of fundamental physics. Storing a bit of information requires energy to combat thermal fluctuations and entropy. As we approach the limits of atomic storage, a radical paradigm shift is required.

evidence.title: Optimisation of energy and exergy of two-spool turbofan engines using genetic algorithms
evidence.abstract: This paper presents an application of Genetic Algorithm (GA) metaheuristics to optimise the design of two-spool turbofan engines based on exergy and energy theories. The GA is used to seek the optimal values of eight parameters that define the turbofan engine. These parameters are encoded as chromosomes (a metaphor) in GA. A computer program called TurboJet-Engine Optimizer v1.0 (TJEO-1.0) was developed by the authors to perform calculations of thermodynamic properties of the engine and implement the optimisations. The caloric properties of the working fluids are obtained by using an 8th-order polynomial fluid model taken from an existing literature. The turbo-mechanical components in the turbofan engine are as well assumed to exhibit polytropic efficiencies of today's technology level. The TJEO-1.0 is integrated with Pyevolve, an open source GA optimisation framework built for used with Python programming language. The optimal design created by TJEO-1.0 was evaluated with the following criteria: (1.) energy efficiency, (2.) exergy efficiency, and (3.) combination of both of them. The results suggest that the design of turbofan engine optimised based on the third criterion is able to produce higher specific thrust (by more than 30 %), compared with the ones optimised based on the first and the second criteria.

evidence.title: A single-atom heat engine
evidence.abstract: Heat engines convert thermal energy into mechanical work and generally involve a large number of particles. We report the experimental realization of a single-atom heat engine. An ion is confined in a linear Paul trap with tapered geometry and driven thermally by coupling it alternately to hot and cold reservoirs. The output power of the engine is used to drive a harmonic oscillation. From direct measurements of the ion dynamics, we were able to determine the thermodynamic cycles for various temperature differences of the reservoirs. We then used these cycles to evaluate the power P and efficiency η of the engine, obtaining values up to P = 3.4 × 10(-22)joules per second and η = 0.28%, consistent with analytical estimations. Our results demonstrate that thermal machines can be reduced to the limit of single atoms.

evidence.title: The atmospheric steam engine as energy converter for low and medium temperature thermal energy
evidence.abstract: Many industrial processes and renewable energy sources produce thermal energy with temperatures below 100 °C. The cost-effective generation of mechanical energy from this thermal energy still constitutes an engineering problem. The atmospheric steam engine is a very simple machine which employs the steam generated by boiling water at atmospheric pressures. Its main disadvantage is the low theoretical efficiency of 0.064. In this article, first the theory of the atmospheric steam engine is extended to show that operation for temperatures between 60 °C and 100 °C is possible although efficiencies are further reduced. Second, the addition of a forced expansion stroke, where the steam volume is increased using external energy, is shown to lead to significantly increased overall efficiencies ranging from 0.084 for a boiler temperature of T0 = 60 °C to 0.25 for T0 = 100 °C. The simplicity of the machine indicates cost-effectiveness. The theoretical work shows that the atmospheric steam engine still has development potential.<br/

evidence.title: Modelling and experimentation on air hybrid engine concepts for automotive applications
evidence.abstract:
This thesis was submitted for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy and awarded by Brunel University.Hybrid powertrains that use compressed air to help power a vehicle could dramatically improve the fuel economy, particularly in cities and urban areas where the traffic conditions involve a lot of starts and stops. In such conditions, a large amount of fuel is needed to accelerate the vehicle, and much of this is converted to heat in brake friction during decelerations. Capturing, storing and reusing this braking energy to produce additional power can therefore improve fuel efficiency.
In this study, three approaches towards air hybrid powertrains are proposed and analyzed. In the first approach, an energy recovery valve or two shut-off valves connected to a convenient access hole on the engine cylinder is proposed to enable the cylinder to operate as a regenerative compressor and/or expander when required. In the second approach, one of the exhaust valves in an engine equipped with a Fully Variable Valve Actuation (FVVA) system is pneumatically or hydraulically operated as a dedicated gas transfer valve connected to an air reservoir. The third approach combines the advantages of the conventional valvetrain’s simplicity with emerging production technologies. In order to achieve this, two well established technologies are used in addition to valve deactivation; Variable Valve Timing (VVT) and/or Cam Profile Switching (CPS). Provided that a conventional, camshaft-operated variable valvetrain is used, the need of adopting fully variable valve actuation is eliminated and thus only minor modifications to the engine architecture are required.
The aforementioned concepts are described in details. Some basic principles of their operation are also discussed in order to provide a better understanding on how fuel economy is achieved by means of engine hybridization and regenerative braking. Both experimental and computational results are presented and compared. Finally, a vehicle and driveline model, which simulates the operation of a typical passenger vehicle in urban driving conditions and predicts the efficiency of the energy regeneration, has been set up and used to study the effects of the application of each air hybrid concept on the vehicle’s energy usage throughout the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) and the 10-15 driving cycle.

candidates.mechanism: A low-thermal-effusivity coating on the combustion chamber walls (piston crown, firedeck, valve faces) makes the wall surface temperature swing dynamically with the in-cylinder gas temperature instead of staying pinned near coolant temperature. During combustion and expansion the surface runs hotter, shrinking the gas-to-wall temperature gradient exactly when heat loss costs the most work; during intake and compression it runs cooler, so the fresh charge is not over-heated. Less fuel energy is therefore lost to the cooling system and more remains as indicated work.
candidates.intervention: Apply a sub-millimeter, functionally graded low-effusivity coating (micro-porous ceramic/metal-ceramic composite) to the piston crown and cylinder-head firedeck, with effusivity and thickness tuned so the surface-temperature swing amplitude and phase track the in-cylinder gas temperature swing. Coolant circuit, exhaust manifold, aftertreatment, and ECU calibration remain untouched.
candidates.predicted_effect: At identical steady-state load points, total heat rejection to coolant plus exhaust drops (target 3–8%) while brake thermal efficiency rises by a corresponding amount, with no increase in NOx, no change in fuel compatibility, and no loss of power density.
candidates.testable_prediction: Run coated and uncoated engines back-to-back on a dynamometer at fixed load/speed points, measuring coolant and exhaust heat rejection, brake thermal efficiency, fuel flow, and NOx; the child is killed if total waste-heat rejection does not fall while NOx and fuel flow stay flat.
candidates.mechanism_source_span: integrating a high-power radiative cooling film as the cool end of TEGs to enable a large and continuous temperature difference
candidates.support_state_note: IMPROVE_CHILD_SUPPORT_NOT_ADJUDICATED: the child's mutated mechanism has no mechanism-space evidence adjudication; the release gate holds non-affirmative support states (R401 Phase 4)

derivation_trace.causal_change: The parent tried to recover waste heat after it had already left the working fluid, which required a sky-facing radiative cold side (infeasible in a hot engine bay, weak transfer to under-hood conditions), exhaust-manifold hardware (regulatory incompatibility with emissions/OBD systems), and the pairing of TEG with radiative film (an obvious combination). The child changes the causal target from recovery to prevention: it stops the heat from leaving the working fluid by tuning the wall's thermal effusivity. This removes the cold-side requirement entirely, needs no exhaust-side component, is one physical mechanism rather than a combination of two devices, and transfers to any engine because wall heat-transfer loss is universal.
derivation_trace.novel_design_variable: Combustion-chamber wall thermal effusivity (sqrt(k·rho·c_p)) and the resulting surface-temperature swing amplitude and phase — the parent varied only TEG placement and cold-side emissivity.

hard_blocks.physical_constraint: CSF turnover rate = 2.88x/day = 259 turnovers in 90 days. No membrane or affinity mechanism can overcome this. The ceiling is PHYSIOLOGICAL (CSF production rate is a constant).
hard_blocks.lesson: Before investing in any retention mechanism, check the CSF TURNOVER RATE. The turnover rate (2.88x/day) is a physiological constant that makes long-term retention physically impossible for any membrane-based mechanism.

warnings.mechanism: R2-C3 predictor v1 — pressure-trajectory + phenotype classification for VSS failure-type prediction
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM (sharpened per CEO Round 56o): 'Existing information + existing transformation + existing control, merely recombined, is insufficient. A combination qualifies only if it produces a demonstrably new technical effect that survives prior art and non-obviousness attack. A world-class invention needs a genuinely new technical information source, transformation, or control capability. Do not build an AI layer on top of an already-claimed sensing/control architecture.' NOTE: This theorem does NOT create a universal 'new sensor required' rule. A novel combination of existing measurements CAN qualify if it produces a new, technically non-obvious effect. The theorem rejects TRIVIAL recombination, not all combinations.
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.territory: CV-T05 (R2-C3 phenotype discovery, Round 56 orthogonal search)
warnings.mechanism: OSV-4: HRV/autonomic state as orthogonal predictor for R2-C3
warnings.lesson: A signal can be GENUINELY ORTHOGONAL to a specific measurement architecture (Hakim measures pressure, not HRV) and still be a DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE of the same physiological variable (ICP → sympathetic → HRV). Orthogonality to one architecture does not imply independence from the underlying physiology. Before claiming a signal is 'new information,' test whether it is causally downstream of an already-measured variable. If A → B and A is measured, then B is a proxy for A, not new information — even if B is measured by a different sensor.
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.mechanism: RES-4 broad: adaptive cerebrospinal venous stent with sensing + flow regulation
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-014: 'No result for our formulation is not evidence that the capability is absent. Patent searches must generate terminology from patent claims + descriptions + CPC classes + inventor vocabulary + adjacent technologies, not just internally coined phrases. A query-fragile search produces false negatives.' The machine must be better at discovering what competitors actually claimed than it is at inventing elegant names for what we hope is new.
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.mechanism: Stroke: clot-vessel adhesion isolation + measurement + strategy selection (Layer A: force-decomposition estimator v1)
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Stroke Round 58; applies to all latent-variable inventions)
warnings.mechanism: Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough — adversarial model-uncertainty and practical-operation survival are mandatory
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-017: A discovery engine earns trust when it attacks its own successful proof harder than its unsuccessful ideas. Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

informational.lesson: Any anti-fouling mechanism that relies on flow direction must be tested against RETROGRADE flow. Retrograde flow is a realistic clinical scenario (cough, Valsalva, venous pressure changes).

informational.mechanism: M3_REFINED electrothermal SMA retrieval
informational.lesson: ALWAYS report worst-case reliability for clinical devices. Averages mask catastrophic failure modes. Thermal activation in a 37°C body environment has a narrow window (37-45°C = 8°C max). Sensor electronics are a SPOF that cannot be fully resolved by redundancy (common-mode failures).

informational.mechanism: M5_REFINED adaptive over-drainage controller (sleep-state + venous pressure)
informational.lesson: Do not assume VP shunt problems apply to the eShunt. The eShunt's drainage geometry is fundamentally different (short path, no siphon). Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry. Over-drainage is siphon-driven; without a hydrostatic column, it may not occur.

informational.mechanism: Flow reversal obstruction clearing (R3)
informational.lesson: Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Governed by the second law of thermodynamics, waste heat generation is inevitable and has been a major source of energy loss and environmental concern in human society. Harvesting waste heat into useful energy has thus become a paramount priority, but has remained challenging with efficiency and cost constraints. Thermoelectric generators (TEGs), which convert heat into electricity whenever there is a temperature difference, play a crucial role in waste heat harvesting. However, sustaining the temperature difference for uninterrupted and high-power density electricity generation is a major challenge in TEGs to achieve practical applications due to the thermal equilibrium. Here, we demonstrate a diurnal waste heat harvester by integrating a high-power radiative cooling film as the cool end of TEGs to enable a large and continuous temperature difference. Significant voltage increase from 30.0 mV to 65.7 mV was achieved, leading to a dramatic power density enhancement of 4.8 times from 35.2 mW m−2 to 168.6 mW m−2. In an open zone, an ultra-high power density of 2.76 W m−2 was achieved at a heat source temperature of 80 °C, exceeding the performance of state-of-the-art radiatively cooled TEGs. More importantly, a portable and foldable thermal energy harvesting prototype composed of 24 TEGs arranged in an array has been constructed. When attached to a hot object (e.g. a car engine hood), it can output 5 V to charge personal electronics (e.g. a cellphone), making it a promising practical device for harvesting waste heat in a wide range of outdoor applications.

custody_records.raw_content: Abstract Automobile emissions are significantly dependent on the after‐treatment system performance, which is partly determined by exhaust temperature. Regarding diesel passenger cars, after‐treatment systems generally include diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC), diesel particulate filter (DPF), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR). The layouts affect their temperature variations because of the heat loss and thermal capacity of tailpipes and after‐treatment systems. As for the original layout of DOC+DPF+SCR, nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions are the main concerns of diesel vehicle emissions, especially under cold‐start conditions. Ammonia Creation and Conversion Technology (ACCT) system shows excellent performance of reducing cold‐start NOx emissions; additionally, the damage costs of individual exhaust emissions are different greatly, which may change the priority of emission reductions when considering monetary penalty. In this article, the impacts of the after‐treatment system layouts on the exhaust emission reductions were investigated based on a diesel passenger car; additionally, SCR and ACCT systems as the De‐NOx devices were adopted individually in corresponding scenarios; the after‐treatment system layouts were assessed from the viewpoints of both emission factors and monetary penalty. The results indicated that the ACCT system presented much better NOx reduction effectiveness than SCR system over different layouts. NOx reduction efficiency was very sensitive to vehicle operation conditions over the upstream layouts of NOx reduction devices. The layout‐1 of DOC+ACCT+DPF showed the lowest global emission factors from the diesel passenger car. DPF was much easier to achieve regeneration under the original layout conditions due to its shortest distance to the engine. The layout‐2 of ACCT+DOC+DPF had the minimum monetary penalty factor of exhaust emissions from this diesel passenger car.

custody_records.raw_content: Nanofluids offer superior heat transfer compared to conventional automotive coolants, with further improvements achievable through particle hybridization and particle shape effects. This study numerically investigates the thermal performance of a ruffled-fin radiator using ternary hybrid nanofluids composed of ZnO, Al 2 O 3 , TiO 2 , MWCNTs, graphene, Fe, Cu, and Ag nanoparticles at varying volume fractions. Combinations such as Fe/Cu/Ag, Fe/Cu/ZnO, and Ag/Al 2 O 3 /TiO 2 enhanced convective heat transfer, as reflected in increased Nusselt numbers and overall heat transfer coefficients. Increasing the volume fraction reduced outlet coolant temperature, with an optimal nanofluid achieving a 44.6% temperature drop at the engine outlet. The performance index, defined as a composite measure of heat transfer and cooling efficiency, decreased by 5.8-11.7% across the eight ternary nanofluids, with non-metallic oxides exhibiting the smallest reduction. These results demonstrate the role of ternary hybrid nanofluids in improving radiator cooling while indicating efficiency trade-offs at higher volume fractions.

custody_records.raw_content: Thermal radiation, a fundamental heat transfer mechanism, is crucial for energy exchange across various applications. However, conventional radiative heat transfer systems rely on omnidirectional thermal radiation, causing energy dissipation in undesired directions and limiting radiative heat transfer efficiency. Here, we show that perfectly matched directional thermal emission between an emitter and absorber can reach a theoretical efficiency up to 100%. In a parallel-plate configuration, replacing a conventional system with a customized directional system raises efficiency from 29% to 100%. We further experimentally demonstrate directional radiative heat transfer realizes substantial energy savings of 67.8% in vacuum and 28.7% in non-vacuum conditions. Moreover, directional radiative heat transfer enables efficient heating in diverse scenarios, including vehicle heating, car paint drying, human body heating, and rail car thawing, achieving 17-46% energy savings. Our work highlights the broad applicability and energy-saving potential of directional radiative heat transfer, opening new avenues for efficient energy utilization.

custody_records.raw_content: Optimizing passenger thermal comfort while maintaining energy efficiency remains a critical challenge in automotive climate control. This study investigates the complex thermal interaction between a passenger and a car seat, introducing a novel technique for direct thermal management through the vehicle's heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system. An experimental setup was developed using evaporator coils integrated beneath seat surfaces, addressing a significant gap in the literature regarding two-way (heating and cooling) seat thermal management. Artificial Neural Networks were employed to model the ambiguous system parameters and to predict thermal performance. The results show an excellent predictive accuracy with Mean Squared Error of 1.29E-02 and correlation coefficient of 0.99659. The average deviations were under -0.21% for cooling capacity, -0.02% for heating capacity and 0.38% for coefficient of performance. These results show that the integration of intelligent algorithms into modified heating, ventilation, and air conditioning architectures significantly improves occupant comfort and system efficiency, thereby providing a powerful data-driven framework for next-generation automotive climate control solutions.

1. Introduction: The End of Storage and the Rise of Location

1.1 The Crisis of the Von Neumann Bottleneck

The history of computing has been defined by a singular, persistent constraint: the physical limitation of information storage. From the earliest magnetic core memories to modern solid-state arrays, the fundamental paradigm has remained unchanged. Data is treated as a physical object—a sequence of magnetized grains or trapped electrons—that must be generated, moved, written, and maintained. This "containment model" of information has led to the Von Neumann bottleneck, where the speed of processing vastly outstrips the speed of retrieval, and the energy cost of maintaining data entropy threatens the scalability of planetary computation.

As we transition into an era of exascale computing and the burgeoning Internet of Things (IoT), the volume of data is expanding at a rate that physical storage media cannot sustain. The "Crisis of Storage" is not merely a question of capacity; it is a question of fundamental physics. Storing a bit of information requires energy to combat thermal fluctuations and entropy. As we approach the limits of atomic storage, a radical paradigm shift is required.

Deterministic Harmonic Access (DHA) represents this shift. It transitions the industry from a paradigm of storage to a paradigm of location. DHA posits that all finite information already exists within the infinite, non-repeating expansions of irrational constants (such as $\pi$, $e$, or $\sqrt{2}$). Therefore, the act of "saving" a file is not a write operation, but a search operation. The file is not created; its coordinates are discovered. DHA serves as the concrete, existing interface that bridges the gap between the theoretical "Library of Babel" contained within these constants and the practical, high-speed requirements of modern computing.

The core proposition of DHA is "Zero-Data" computing. In this architecture, a user does not store a 4-gigabyte movie file. custody_records.raw_content: This paper presents an application of Genetic Algorithm (GA) metaheuristics to optimise the design of two-spool turbofan engines based on exergy and energy theories. The GA is used to seek the optimal values of eight parameters that define the turbofan engine. These parameters are encoded as chromosomes (a metaphor) in GA. A computer program called TurboJet-Engine Optimizer v1.0 (TJEO-1.0) was developed by the authors to perform calculations of thermodynamic properties of the engine and implement the optimisations. The caloric properties of the working fluids are obtained by using an 8th-order polynomial fluid model taken from an existing literature. The turbo-mechanical components in the turbofan engine are as well assumed to exhibit polytropic efficiencies of today's technology level. The TJEO-1.0 is integrated with Pyevolve, an open source GA optimisation framework built for used with Python programming language. The optimal design created by TJEO-1.0 was evaluated with the following criteria: (1.) energy efficiency, (2.) exergy efficiency, and (3.) combination of both of them. The results suggest that the design of turbofan engine optimised based on the third criterion is able to produce higher specific thrust (by more than 30 %), compared with the ones optimised based on the first and the second criteria.

custody_records.raw_content: Heat engines convert thermal energy into mechanical work and generally involve a large number of particles. We report the experimental realization of a single-atom heat engine. An ion is confined in a linear Paul trap with tapered geometry and driven thermally by coupling it alternately to hot and cold reservoirs. The output power of the engine is used to drive a harmonic oscillation. From direct measurements of the ion dynamics, we were able to determine the thermodynamic cycles for various temperature differences of the reservoirs. We then used these cycles to evaluate the power P and efficiency η of the engine, obtaining values up to P = 3.4 × 10(-22)joules per second and η = 0.28%, consistent with analytical estimations. Our results demonstrate that thermal machines can be reduced to the limit of single atoms.

custody_records.raw_content: Many industrial processes and renewable energy sources produce thermal energy with temperatures below 100 °C. The cost-effective generation of mechanical energy from this thermal energy still constitutes an engineering problem. The atmospheric steam engine is a very simple machine which employs the steam generated by boiling water at atmospheric pressures. Its main disadvantage is the low theoretical efficiency of 0.064. In this article, first the theory of the atmospheric steam engine is extended to show that operation for temperatures between 60 °C and 100 °C is possible although efficiencies are further reduced. Second, the addition of a forced expansion stroke, where the steam volume is increased using external energy, is shown to lead to significantly increased overall efficiencies ranging from 0.084 for a boiler temperature of T0 = 60 °C to 0.25 for T0 = 100 °C. The simplicity of the machine indicates cost-effectiveness. The theoretical work shows that the atmospheric steam engine still has development potential.<br/

This thesis was submitted for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy and awarded by Brunel University.Hybrid powertrains that use compressed air to help power a vehicle could dramatically improve the fuel economy, particularly in cities and urban areas where the traffic conditions involve a lot of starts and stops. In such conditions, a large amount of fuel is needed to accelerate the vehicle, and much of this is converted to heat in brake friction during decelerations. Capturing, storing and reusing this braking energy to produce additional power can therefore improve fuel efficiency.
In this study, three approaches towards air hybrid powertrains are proposed and analyzed. In the first approach, an energy recovery valve or two shut-off valves connected to a convenient access hole on the engine cylinder is proposed to enable the cylinder to operate as a regenerative compressor and/or expander when required. In the second approach, one of the exhaust valves in an engine equipped with a Fully Variable Valve Actuation (FVVA) system is pneumatically or hydraulically operated as a dedicated gas transfer valve connected to an air reservoir. The third approach combines the advantages of the conventional valvetrain’s simplicity with emerging production technologies. In order to achieve this, two well established technologies are used in addition to valve deactivation; Variable Valve Timing (VVT) and/or Cam Profile Switching (CPS). Provided that a conventional, camshaft-operated variable valvetrain is used, the need of adopting fully variable valve actuation is eliminated and thus only minor modifications to the engine architecture are required.
The aforementioned concepts are described in details. Some basic principles of their operation are also discussed in order to provide a better understanding on how fuel economy is achieved by means of engine hybridization and regenerative braking. Less fuel energy is therefore lost to the cooling system and more remains as indicated work.

doi:10.1016/j.matre.2025.100398.title: High-power radiatively cooled thermoelectric generator for diurnal waste heat harvesting
doi:10.1016/j.matre.2025.100398.abstract: Governed by the second law of thermodynamics, waste heat generation is inevitable and has been a major source of energy loss and environmental concern in human society. Harvesting waste heat into useful energy has thus become a paramount priority, but has remained challenging with efficiency and cost constraints. Thermoelectric generators (TEGs), which convert heat into electricity whenever there is a temperature difference, play a crucial role in waste heat harvesting. However, sustaining the temperature difference for uninterrupted and high-power density electricity generation is a major challenge in TEGs to achieve practical applications due to the thermal equilibrium. Here, we demonstrate a diurnal waste heat harvester by integrating a high-power radiative cooling film as the cool end of TEGs to enable a large and continuous temperature difference. Significant voltage increase from 30.0 mV to 65.7 mV was achieved, leading to a dramatic power density enhancement of 4.8 times from 35.2 mW m−2 to 168.6 mW m−2. In an open zone, an ultra-high power density of 2.76 W m−2 was achieved at a heat source temperature of 80 °C, exceeding the performance of state-of-the-art radiatively cooled TEGs. More importantly, a portable and foldable thermal energy harvesting prototype composed of 24 TEGs arranged in an array has been constructed. When attached to a hot object (e.g. a car engine hood), it can output 5 V to charge personal electronics (e.g. a cellphone), making it a promising practical device for harvesting waste heat in a wide range of outdoor applications.

doi:10.1002/ese3.1001.title: Impacts of De‐NOx system layouts of a diesel passenger car on exhaust emission factors and monetary penalty
doi:10.1002/ese3.1001.abstract: Abstract Automobile emissions are significantly dependent on the after‐treatment system performance, which is partly determined by exhaust temperature. Regarding diesel passenger cars, after‐treatment systems generally include diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC), diesel particulate filter (DPF), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR). The layouts affect their temperature variations because of the heat loss and thermal capacity of tailpipes and after‐treatment systems. As for the original layout of DOC+DPF+SCR, nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions are the main concerns of diesel vehicle emissions, especially under cold‐start conditions. Ammonia Creation and Conversion Technology (ACCT) system shows excellent performance of reducing cold‐start NOx emissions; additionally, the damage costs of individual exhaust emissions are different greatly, which may change the priority of emission reductions when considering monetary penalty. In this article, the impacts of the after‐treatment system layouts on the exhaust emission reductions were investigated based on a diesel passenger car; additionally, SCR and ACCT systems as the De‐NOx devices were adopted individually in corresponding scenarios; the after‐treatment system layouts were assessed from the viewpoints of both emission factors and monetary penalty. The results indicated that the ACCT system presented much better NOx reduction effectiveness than SCR system over different layouts. NOx reduction efficiency was very sensitive to vehicle operation conditions over the upstream layouts of NOx reduction devices. The layout‐1 of DOC+ACCT+DPF showed the lowest global emission factors from the diesel passenger car. DPF was much easier to achieve regeneration under the original layout conditions due to its shortest distance to the engine. The layout‐2 of ACCT+DOC+DPF had the minimum monetary penalty factor of exhaust emissions from this diesel passenger car.

doi:10.1038/s41598-025-26764-w.title: Optimized nanofluid coolants enhance thermal performance in ruffled fin automotive radiators.
doi:10.1038/s41598-025-26764-w.abstract: Nanofluids offer superior heat transfer compared to conventional automotive coolants, with further improvements achievable through particle hybridization and particle shape effects. This study numerically investigates the thermal performance of a ruffled-fin radiator using ternary hybrid nanofluids composed of ZnO, Al 2 O 3 , TiO 2 , MWCNTs, graphene, Fe, Cu, and Ag nanoparticles at varying volume fractions. Combinations such as Fe/Cu/Ag, Fe/Cu/ZnO, and Ag/Al 2 O 3 /TiO 2 enhanced convective heat transfer, as reflected in increased Nusselt numbers and overall heat transfer coefficients. Increasing the volume fraction reduced outlet coolant temperature, with an optimal nanofluid achieving a 44.6% temperature drop at the engine outlet. The performance index, defined as a composite measure of heat transfer and cooling efficiency, decreased by 5.8-11.7% across the eight ternary nanofluids, with non-metallic oxides exhibiting the smallest reduction. These results demonstrate the role of ternary hybrid nanofluids in improving radiator cooling while indicating efficiency trade-offs at higher volume fractions.

doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76043-z.title: Directional thermal emission enables efficient energy savings.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76043-z.abstract: Thermal radiation, a fundamental heat transfer mechanism, is crucial for energy exchange across various applications. However, conventional radiative heat transfer systems rely on omnidirectional thermal radiation, causing energy dissipation in undesired directions and limiting radiative heat transfer efficiency. Here, we show that perfectly matched directional thermal emission between an emitter and absorber can reach a theoretical efficiency up to 100%. In a parallel-plate configuration, replacing a conventional system with a customized directional system raises efficiency from 29% to 100%. We further experimentally demonstrate directional radiative heat transfer realizes substantial energy savings of 67.8% in vacuum and 28.7% in non-vacuum conditions. Moreover, directional radiative heat transfer enables efficient heating in diverse scenarios, including vehicle heating, car paint drying, human body heating, and rail car thawing, achieving 17-46% energy savings. Our work highlights the broad applicability and energy-saving potential of directional radiative heat transfer, opening new avenues for efficient energy utilization.

doi:10.1007/s10973-026-15752-5.title: Optimization of automotive HVAC performance and passenger comfort through intelligent algorithms.
doi:10.1007/s10973-026-15752-5.abstract: Optimizing passenger thermal comfort while maintaining energy efficiency remains a critical challenge in automotive climate control. This study investigates the complex thermal interaction between a passenger and a car seat, introducing a novel technique for direct thermal management through the vehicle's heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system. An experimental setup was developed using evaporator coils integrated beneath seat surfaces, addressing a significant gap in the literature regarding two-way (heating and cooling) seat thermal management. Artificial Neural Networks were employed to model the ambiguous system parameters and to predict thermal performance. The results show an excellent predictive accuracy with Mean Squared Error of 1.29E-02 and correlation coefficient of 0.99659. The average deviations were under -0.21% for cooling capacity, -0.02% for heating capacity and 0.38% for coefficient of performance. These results show that the integration of intelligent algorithms into modified heating, ventilation, and air conditioning architectures significantly improves occupant comfort and system efficiency, thereby providing a powerful data-driven framework for next-generation automotive climate control solutions.

doi:10.5281/zenodo.18307054.title: Deterministic Harmonic Access (DHA): The Unified Interface for Recursive Computational Stability and Infinite State Retrieval
doi:10.5281/zenodo.18307054.abstract:
Deterministic Harmonic Access (DHA): The Unified Interface for Recursive Computational Stability and Infinite State Retrieval

1. Introduction: The End of Storage and the Rise of Location

1.1 The Crisis of the Von Neumann Bottleneck

The history of computing has been defined by a singular, persistent constraint: the physical limitation of information storage. From the earliest magnetic core memories to modern solid-state arrays, the fundamental paradigm has remained unchanged. Data is treated as a physical object—a sequence of magnetized grains or trapped electrons—that must be generated, moved, written, and maintained. This "containment model" of information has led to the Von Neumann bottleneck, where the speed of processing vastly outstrips the speed of retrieval, and the energy cost of maintaining data entropy threatens the scalability of planetary computation.

As we transition into an era of exascale computing and the burgeoning Internet of Things (IoT), the volume of data is expanding at a rate that physical storage media cannot sustain. The "Crisis of Storage" is not merely a question of capacity; it is a question of fundamental physics. Storing a bit of information requires energy to combat thermal fluctuations and entropy. As we approach the limits of atomic storage, a radical paradigm shift is required.

Deterministic Harmonic Access (DHA) represents this shift. It transitions the industry from a paradigm of storage to a paradigm of location. DHA posits that all finite information already exists within the infinite, non-repeating expansions of irrational constants (such as $\pi$, $e$, or $\sqrt{2}$). Therefore, the act of "saving" a file is not a write operation, but a search operation. The file is not created; its coordinates are discovered. DHA serves as the concrete, existing interface that bridges the gap between the theoretical "Library of Babel" contained within these constants and the practical, high-speed requirements of modern computing.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.1207.0743.title: Optimisation of energy and exergy of two-spool turbofan engines using genetic algorithms
doi:10.48550/arxiv.1207.0743.abstract: This paper presents an application of Genetic Algorithm (GA) metaheuristics to optimise the design of two-spool turbofan engines based on exergy and energy theories. The GA is used to seek the optimal values of eight parameters that define the turbofan engine. These parameters are encoded as chromosomes (a metaphor) in GA. A computer program called TurboJet-Engine Optimizer v1.0 (TJEO-1.0) was developed by the authors to perform calculations of thermodynamic properties of the engine and implement the optimisations. The caloric properties of the working fluids are obtained by using an 8th-order polynomial fluid model taken from an existing literature. The turbo-mechanical components in the turbofan engine are as well assumed to exhibit polytropic efficiencies of today's technology level. The TJEO-1.0 is integrated with Pyevolve, an open source GA optimisation framework built for used with Python programming language. The optimal design created by TJEO-1.0 was evaluated with the following criteria: (1.) energy efficiency, (2.) exergy efficiency, and (3.) combination of both of them. The results suggest that the design of turbofan engine optimised based on the third criterion is able to produce higher specific thrust (by more than 30 %), compared with the ones optimised based on the first and the second criteria.

doi:10.1126/science.aad6320.title: A single-atom heat engine
doi:10.1126/science.aad6320.abstract: Heat engines convert thermal energy into mechanical work and generally involve a large number of particles. We report the experimental realization of a single-atom heat engine. An ion is confined in a linear Paul trap with tapered geometry and driven thermally by coupling it alternately to hot and cold reservoirs. The output power of the engine is used to drive a harmonic oscillation. From direct measurements of the ion dynamics, we were able to determine the thermodynamic cycles for various temperature differences of the reservoirs. We then used these cycles to evaluate the power P and efficiency η of the engine, obtaining values up to P = 3.4 × 10(-22)joules per second and η = 0.28%, consistent with analytical estimations. Our results demonstrate that thermal machines can be reduced to the limit of single atoms.

doi:10.1016/j.renene.2012.10.056.title: The atmospheric steam engine as energy converter for low and medium temperature thermal energy
doi:10.1016/j.renene.2012.10.056.abstract: Many industrial processes and renewable energy sources produce thermal energy with temperatures below 100 °C. The cost-effective generation of mechanical energy from this thermal energy still constitutes an engineering problem. The atmospheric steam engine is a very simple machine which employs the steam generated by boiling water at atmospheric pressures. Its main disadvantage is the low theoretical efficiency of 0.064. In this article, first the theory of the atmospheric steam engine is extended to show that operation for temperatures between 60 °C and 100 °C is possible although efficiencies are further reduced. Second, the addition of a forced expansion stroke, where the steam volume is increased using external energy, is shown to lead to significantly increased overall efficiencies ranging from 0.084 for a boiler temperature of T0 = 60 °C to 0.25 for T0 = 100 °C. The simplicity of the machine indicates cost-effectiveness. The theoretical work shows that the atmospheric steam engine still has development potential.<br/

title:ca95ea55e71dd29c.title: Modelling and experimentation on air hybrid engine concepts for automotive applications
title:ca95ea55e71dd29c.abstract:
This thesis was submitted for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy and awarded by Brunel University.Hybrid powertrains that use compressed air to help power a vehicle could dramatically improve the fuel economy, particularly in cities and urban areas where the traffic conditions involve a lot of starts and stops. In such conditions, a large amount of fuel is needed to accelerate the vehicle, and much of this is converted to heat in brake friction during decelerations. Capturing, storing and reusing this braking energy to produce additional power can therefore improve fuel efficiency.
In this study, three approaches towards air hybrid powertrains are proposed and analyzed. In the first approach, an energy recovery valve or two shut-off valves connected to a convenient access hole on the engine cylinder is proposed to enable the cylinder to operate as a regenerative compressor and/or expander when required. In the second approach, one of the exhaust valves in an engine equipped with a Fully Variable Valve Actuation (FVVA) system is pneumatically or hydraulically operated as a dedicated gas transfer valve connected to an air reservoir. The third approach combines the advantages of the conventional valvetrain’s simplicity with emerging production technologies. In order to achieve this, two well established technologies are used in addition to valve deactivation; Variable Valve Timing (VVT) and/or Cam Profile Switching (CPS). Provided that a conventional, camshaft-operated variable valvetrain is used, the need of adopting fully variable valve actuation is eliminated and thus only minor modifications to the engine architecture are required.
The aforementioned concepts are described in details. Some basic principles of their operation are also discussed in order to provide a better understanding on how fuel economy is achieved by means of engine hybridization and regenerative braking. Both experimental and computational results are presented and compared. Finally, a vehicle and driveline model, which simulates the operation of a typical passenger vehicle in urban driving conditions and predicts the efficiency of the energy regeneration, has been set up and used to study the effects of the application of each air hybrid concept on the vehicle’s energy usage throughout the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) and the 10-15 driving cycle.

design_inputs.input: Mechanism driver (proposed)
design_inputs.value: A low-thermal-effusivity coating on the combustion chamber walls (piston crown, firedeck, valve faces) makes the wall surface temperature swing dynamically with the in-cylinder gas temperature instead of staying pinned near coolant temperature. During combustion and expansion the surface runs hotter, shrinking the gas-to-wall temperature gradient exactly when heat loss costs the most work; during intake and compression it runs cooler, so the fresh charge is not over-heated. Less fuel energy is therefore lost to the cooling system and more remains as indicated work.

proposed_design.input: must remain practical for automotive propulsion including power density, emissions, and fuel compatibility
proposed_design.mechanism: A low-thermal-effusivity coating on the combustion chamber walls (piston crown, firedeck, valve faces) makes the wall surface temperature swing dynamically with the in-cylinder gas temperature instead of staying pinned near coolant temperature. During combustion and expansion the surface runs hotter, shrinking the gas-to-wall temperature gradient exactly when heat loss costs the most work; during intake and compression it runs cooler, so the fresh charge is not over-heated. Less fuel energy is therefore lost to the cooling system and more remains as indicated work.

From the earliest magnetic core memories to modern solid-state arrays, the fundamental paradigm has remained unchanged. Data is treated as a physical object—a sequence of magnetized grains or trapped electrons—that must be generated, moved, written, and maintained. This "containment model" of information has led to the Von Neumann bottleneck, where the speed of processing vastly outstrips the speed of retrieval, and the energy cost of maintaining data entropy threatens the scalability of planetary computation.\n\nAs we transition into an era of exascale computing and the burgeoning Internet of Things (IoT), the volume of data is expanding at a rate that physical storage media cannot sustain. The "Crisis of Storage" is not merely a question of capacity; it is a question of fundamental physics. Storing a bit of information requires energy to combat thermal fluctuations and entropy. As we approach the limits of atomic storage, a radical paradigm shift is required.\n\nDeterministic Harmonic Access (DHA) represents this shift. It transitions the industry from a paradigm of storage to a paradigm of location. DHA posits that all finite information already exists within the infinite, non-repeating expansions of irrational constants (such as $\\pi$, $e$, or $\\sqrt{2}$). Therefore, the act of "saving" a file is not a write operation, but a search operation. The file is not created; its coordinates are discovered. DHA serves as the concrete, existing interface that bridges the gap between the theoretical "Library of Babel" contained within these constants and the practical, high-speed requirements of modern computing.\n\n1.2 The DHA Proposition: Zero-Data Computing\n\nThe core proposition of DHA is "Zero-Data" computing.
